rationale: Matthew 15:30-31 lists "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute" and ends with "the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing" (BSB). Isaiah 35:5-6 promises that "the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer" (BSB). Three Greek nouns are shared with the Septuagint of Isaiah 35:5-6: typhlos (blind), kophos and cholos (lame). But kophos means "mute" in Matthew 15:31 (the kophoi are "speaking") and "deaf" in Isaiah 35:5, and none of the verbs match: Matthew's peripatountas and blepontas against the Septuagint's haleitai and anoichthesontai. Gill (via the Biblehub aggregator) says these cures were "as was prophesied of the times of the Messiah" and cites Isaiah 35:5, without further argument. Graded plausible, following conn-matt9-blind-isaiah35, and below conn-matt11-blind-isaiah35 (strong), whose 11:5 matches three groups and one full verb-noun pairing. Matthew uses no formula here. Mark's account of the same journey has one healing, of a man "deaf and hardly able to speak" (Mark 7:32, BSB); Meyer notes that Mark's word for him, mogilalon, is the Septuagint's word in Isaiah 35:6 (a reading of Mark, not of Matthew).
